column3: The challenge to mute idols gives a close parallel: claimed agents cannot answer, and their mute state itself exposes the claim.
Frames the scene as an appointed Day of Separation, the judicial setting in which 77:35's silence occurs.
The demand that idols be asked whether they speak closely parallels speechlessness as exposure of a false claim; the arranged objects also remain evidentiary signs.
Its exclusion of wealth and sons on that day only broadly supports the loss of ordinary means of defense.
The immediate command to proceed toward what was denied places the silence within compelled confrontation.
An irrevocable appointed day supplies the fixed occasion for the loss of speech, without itself specifying silence.
Directly joins fulfilled judgment for wrongdoing with "they do not speak," making deeds rather than a renewed counter-account decisive.
The immediately preceding woe identifies the silent group as deniers under judgment.
Contrasts speech not proceeding from desire with the blocked speech of 77:35; it also leaves open meaningful communication beyond ordinary voiced utterance.
Names the denied Day of Separation, clarifying the forensic occasion of 77:35.
Its immediate continuation says they are not permitted, hence cannot offer excuses, specifying the procedural force of 77:35.
Depicts "today" as a punitive condition of isolation, supporting an event-day rather than a mere calendar date.
The deniers' compelled recognition of the Day of Recompense precedes the kind of judgment in which denial can no longer be recast.
Life and death establish the resurrection horizon but add little about speech or defense.
Speech is granted to birds, setting a counterpoint in which nonhuman utterance is possible while judged deniers may be mute.
The nearby assembly of later and earlier people on the Day of Separation supplies the public hearing-context for their silence.
The next compelled movement into the false shade continues the judgment scene surrounding the silence.
A record that speaks with truth provides an alternate evidentiary voice when persons cannot speak, while insisting on non-injustice.
Their admission that the idols do not speak directly sharpens the contrast between exposed mute objects and human accountability.
The repeated nearby woe keeps the silence tied to the deniers' judgment.
Bodily witnesses speak against their owners, preserving the possibility that material evidence testifies when defendants' speech is unavailable.
Calls the punitive welcome their provision on the Day of Recompense, adding the settled outcome of the same judgment horizon.
The bare introduction to the deniers' saying only begins a nearby denial sequence.
Unanswering objects until resurrection form a limited parallel to failed response, with the final gathering exposing their actual relation to calls.
The refusal to alter revelation and fear of a great day relate speech to authority, but not the defendants' silence directly.
The denial that the shade protects continues the punitive scene immediately after 77:35.
Their question about when the Day of Recompense is treats the event as challengeable or deferrable, later answered by its arrival.
The absence of vain speech in the other outcome supplies a restrained contrast, not a direct account of forensic silence.
The challenge to use any scheme follows the silence and shows that resistance has reached its limit.
Compares the promised truth to the certainty of human speech, counterbalancing 77:35's inability to speak; signs may also bear meaning without words.
Universal exposure with nothing concealed supports a setting where concealment and defensive speech lose force.
Another immediate woe reinforces the judgment against the deniers in the silent scene.
The book speaks truth against people from what they did, a direct evidentiary counterpart to their inability to speak.
The deniers call it a difficult day while rushing toward the caller, illustrating compelled arrival at the event.
The great seizure presents the day as decisive punitive execution, though it does not specify speech.
The day reverses even closest relations, broadly supporting the collapse of ordinary supports and responses.
The great day of rising before the Lord supplies the formal accountability horizon for silence and testimony.
The continuing fire image situates the silence in the same unfolding consequence.
The Day of Recompense is where recorded conduct becomes endured outcome, a broad context for speech no longer changing the case.
A private plan to exclude the needy "today" does not materially clarify 77:35.
The final fire comparison continues the immediate scene around the silent deniers.
Its emphasis on the unknowable magnitude of the Day of Recompense supports the exceptional event-setting, weakly.
The announced identification of the formerly denied reality parallels 77:35's completed exposure.
Generic denial by a former people supplies only a distant denier pattern.
Today they are surrendered, an outcome-state compatible with the inability to mount a response.
A historical "difficult day" conveys distress but no judicial silence.
The protected outcome for the mindful is a remote contrast to the deniers' scene.
The grim day both names an overwhelming event and, in the linked reading, motivates present conduct; this preserves an outcome-oriented parallel rather than silence itself.
The promised day becomes directly addressed as "your day," highlighting arrival and allocation of the awaited event.
Appeal to ancestral custom is only a general form of denial that later judgment can overturn.
Delay until resurrection marks a bounded interval but does not explain the silence at judgment.
The Master of the Day of Recompense establishes the governing judicial horizon in which speech and excuse are constrained.
The desired fruits of the mindful provide a distant intra-surah contrast to the deniers' punitive, speechless scene.
The question of what day the messengers are deferred for leads directly to the Day of Separation.
On that day truthfulness benefits the truthful, a useful counterpoint to the deniers' inability to present a defense.
The nearby reward for prior deeds contrasts with the deniers' punitive sequence but adds little to silence.
The known appointed time emphasizes that the final reckoning has a fixed boundary.
The promised day carries both assurance and threat, situating 77:35 in a shared but divergent final appointment.
The claim that there is only one death is a denial backdrop, not evidence about silence.
Fear of a great day's punishment is a broad ethical horizon without a speech connection.
Entrance of a group into the Fire adds only a distant punitive setting.
The general recompense of good-doers does not clarify the speech restriction on deniers.
Hope for God and the Last Day guides present imitation but does not illuminate the courtroom condition.
No substitution, ransom, or aid is accepted on that day, supporting the closure of ordinary rescue and defense.
Revelation's source provides only an indirect contrast with human utterance.
Explicitly names the Day of Separation toward which the messengers are deferred, defining the immediate judgment horizon.
Again removes ransom, intercession, and help, supporting the loss of ordinary means to alter the outcome.
The repeated woe after the two adjacent outcomes continues the verdict against deniers.
Confession of denying the Day of Recompense identifies the denial whose final setting is shown in 77:35.
Delay until the Day of Resurrection supplies a temporal horizon but not the silence condition.
Brief enjoyment and criminality state the deniers' present status, only indirectly leading to 77:35.
No person holds power for another and command belongs to God, a judgment condition that limits interpersonal defense.
A later disclosure of an unseen deed offers only a distant pattern of eventual exposure.
The recurring woe remains part of the same denier judgment sequence, though farther from 77:35.
An unsupported claim of limited Fire duration is a faulty spoken assurance, but not a direct parallel to silence.
Prior self-witness blocks a later plea of unawareness, directly relevant to why a defense may fail at resurrection.
Visible faces register a public outcome, offering bodily disclosure alongside the loss of verbal defense.
Woe for those who disbelieve from their promised day parallels the warning formula surrounding 77:35.
The demand for witnesses and rejection of desire-based testimony foregrounds proof and false assertion, relevant to a later evidentiary closure.
Their refusal to bow identifies persistent refusal within the same denier sequence leading through repeated woe.
Past days of punishment make waiting consequential, but do not clarify speech at the final event.
The demand to produce proof and the subsequent turning away form a pre-judgment contrast to later failed defense.
The bright-faced recipients of mercy are only a remote outcome contrast.
The day when secrets are tested supports complete disclosure, reducing any room for concealed counterclaims.
Deniers hear yet fail to understand and dispute with dismissive speech, a pre-judgment contrast to their later silence.
The repeated woe remains connected to the denier refrain but contributes no new speech detail.
A curse lasting until the Day of Recompense gives only the temporal horizon of final settlement.
False verbal declarations about God make speech itself accountable, a relevant contrast to its later restriction.
The first and the last are summoned together, closely supporting the comprehensive assembly behind the Day of Separation.
Fear for a people's great day is broad warning language, not a speech parallel.
Threatened punishment on a great day gives a historical warning but little on 77:35's procedure.
The promised day becomes bodily downcastness and humiliation, showing fulfilled warning as an imposed public state.
A leader brings his people to the Fire on Resurrection Day, adding collective consequence and adverse leadership.
Seeing what was promised compresses the perceived wait, clarifying the transition from delayed warning to realized event.
The tremendous event overwhelms ordinary bodily and social response, a broad setting for loss of speech.
A day of hunger concerns immediate charitable action and does not clarify the final silence.
The isolated act of looking adds no usable connection to 77:35.
Fire as recompense for rejecting signs supplies the consequence of denial but no specific account of speech.
The contrast of living and dead and of hearing is only a remote lexical association with speech.
Family nursing obligations and capacity do not add to the meaning of 77:35.
God's not speaking to a condemned group on resurrection day is a direct, distinct axis of judicial speech-withdrawal alongside 77:35.
The bringing of a witness from every community and of the Messenger as witness supplies the public evidentiary setting for failed self-defense.
The gathering of messengers and the demand for their response establishes an explicit hearing whose testimony constrains the accused.
The gathered deniers are addressed about their alleged associates, showing a judgment-stage in which questioning occurs.
Their sworn denial before God is a necessary contrary reading: 77:35 cannot erase every final-scene utterance, but marks a particular stage or condition of speechlessness.
Humans and jinn answer a question about received messengers, another contrary dialogue that preserves multiple phases of accountability.
Those sent to and the messengers are questioned, placing 77:35 within a larger sequence of inquiry rather than a simple absence of all speech.
The command for each party to remain in place and the separation of associates supplies a formal counterpart to the Day of Separation.
Every soul tests what it sent ahead, supporting a completed evidentiary review before or beyond personal pleading.
When that day comes, no soul speaks except by permission; it directly qualifies 77:35 as restricted speech, not necessarily absolute muteness in every scene.
The dialogue between followers and leaders after they appear before God is contrary evidence that judgment speech can occur in a distinct phase.
When witnesses are raised, disbelievers are not permitted and are not asked to make amends, closely parallel 77:35-36's blocked defense.
Wrongdoers are neither granted reprieve nor allowed to seek satisfaction after punishment is seen, reinforcing the closure of remedial response.
A witness from every community and a Book explaining all things foreground the evidence that supersedes unsupported speech.
Every soul comes pleading for itself, a direct contrary scene that requires 77:35's silence to be read as conditional or sequential.
Each person's record is fastened to them and brought open on resurrection day, supplying written evidence independent of oral defense.
The command to read one's own book makes the self-record sufficient for reckoning, directly relevant to the closure of argument.
The comprehensive gathering leaves none behind, supporting the public assembly assumed by 77:35.
The opened record causes fear and speaks through exhaustive inscription, closely paralleling evidence that makes defenses ineffective.
Voices are humbled before the Merciful and only a faint sound is heard, an acoustic parallel that can coexist with limited permitted speech.
Intercession benefits only one granted permission whose word is approved, directly framing speech at judgment as licensed rather than freely available.
Intercession is limited to those approved, reinforcing the restricted authorization of advocacy in the final assembly.
Kinship does not function through the Trumpet event and people do not question one another, supporting collapse of normal social defense.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify about what people did, a direct counterpart in which embodied evidence speaks against the person.
God questions the objects of worship about misleading servants, preserving another judgment dialogue and thus a differentiated sequence of speech.
The creature's address to people contrasts granted nonhuman speech with the deniers' speechlessness and sustains the material-evidence reading.
The call about alleged partners presents a judgment question that deniers must face.
The question of how messengers were answered directly concerns the response whose opportunity is later closed in 77:35-36.
The repeated call for alleged partners shows an evidentiary challenge that exposes failed claims.
The wrongdoers' excuses do not benefit on that day, directly supports the procedural closure stated beside 77:35.
On the Day of Decision, belief after the fact does not benefit deniers and they are not reprieved, closely matching irreversible judgment.
Intercession is unavailable except after permission, preserving the same authorized-speech framework as 77:36 and related passages.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify, the clearest embodied-evidence parallel to 77:35.
The condemned approach one another questioning, contrary evidence that locates 77:35 within a sequence rather than all final events.
Their accusation that leaders approached from the right continues that contrary judgment dialogue.
Leaders deny coercing their followers, further preserving competing spoken exchanges in the wider final scene.
The disputants contend before their Lord on resurrection day, another contrary courtroom phase rather than a reason to collapse 77:35 into universal silence.
Hearts at throats and wrongdoers lacking an intimate ally or obeyed intercessor depict the constriction and loss of effective advocacy.
The day when wrongdoers' excuse does not benefit them directly supports 77:36's inability to apologize.
Every community is seen kneeling and called to its record, immediately framing the Book that speaks against them in 45:29.
The two receivers record what is received, providing the documentary basis for accountability beyond later self-description.
Every utterance has an attending recorder, making speech itself part of the evidence rather than a free final defense.
Each soul comes with a driver and witness, supporting compelled appearance and external testimony.
The companion presents the prepared record, another concrete evidentiary voice in the final scene.
The divine word is not changed and no injustice occurs, defining a verdict no later argument can revise.
Even angelic intercession has no effect except after divine permission and approval, reinforcing licensed rather than autonomous advocacy.
The hypocrites' plea to believers and the reply to it preserve a contrary post-judgment dialogue, so silence remains contextual.
Their continued exchange about self-deception adds another spoken phase after separation.
Do not make excuses today directly parallels 77:36 and makes the lack of excuse a completed judgment condition.
Receiving the record in the right hand shows the positive counterpart to evidence being publicly handed over.
Receiving the record in the left hand supplies the condemned counterpart, leading into inability to find support.
A person is informed of what was sent ahead and left behind, supporting comprehensive disclosure before defense.
Spirit and angels stand in rows and do not speak except one permitted by the Merciful who speaks rightly, a central direct parallel and qualification.
Noble guardians are assigned over people, supporting the recorded-evidence setting.
The recording agents know what people do, supplying a basis independent of later claims.
Receipt of a record in the right hand provides the positive audit counterpart to final accountability.
Receipt of a record from behind the back supplies the adverse record-bearing counterpart.
The earth reports its news, a direct material-witness parallel in which the scene itself carries evidence.
People emerge separately to be shown their deeds, supporting individualized exposure at the final event.
The smallest good is seen, underscoring the completeness of what can be evidenced.
The smallest evil is seen, likewise limiting the scope for denial or concealment.
God's refusal to speak to those who conceal revelation on resurrection day is a direct parallel to judicial deprivation of speech.
No one intercedes except by permission, supplying the wider authorization rule behind restricted advocacy.
The wrongdoers wish the earth were leveled over them and cannot conceal a report from God, reinforcing total exposure.
The challenge asks who will argue with God on resurrection day, directly framing the final failure of advocacy.
Messengers remove people's argument before God, supplying the evidentiary reason a final defense cannot be reopened.
No ransom can be accepted from the condemned, supporting the collapse of substitute remedies at judgment.
The dying deniers admit their alleged gods have vanished and testify against themselves, a spoken phase that qualifies the silence of 77:35.
Those awaiting the outcome wish for intercession or return, a precluded remedial wish that parallels blocked excuse.
Witnesses declare God's curse on wrongdoers, adding public testimony that overrides their own claims.
Satan's address to his followers after judgment is a clear contrary speech-scene and preserves a sequential reading of 77:35.
The day people come to God is marked by hearing and seeing, a contrast to their earlier blindness and a broad final-scene setting.
The gathering of the mindful as a delegation supplies the positive counterpart to the assembled deniers.
Intercession belongs only to one holding a covenant from the Merciful, reinforcing limited authorized advocacy.
The command to remain in the Fire and not speak to God is a direct later restriction on condemned speech, while also showing that the restriction is addressed within a dialogue.
The divine question about time spent on earth preserves an explicit interrogative stage of final reckoning.
The condemned answer the question, a direct contrary utterance within the same final sequence.
The divine response completes the exchange, confirming that 77:35 concerns a bounded condition rather than all eschatological speech.
The Messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Qur'an supplies an accusatory witness against deniers.
On that day the reports are obscured from them and they do not question one another, a close direct parallel to failed speech and response.
The idolaters have no intercessors among their associates, reinforcing the loss of surrogate advocates.
The Book, prophets, and witnesses are brought and judgment is made in truth, a central evidentiary context for silence.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, confirming that judgment rests on complete knowledge rather than a new verbal account.
The condemned are called and answer in the Fire, a direct contrary dialogue that preserves distinct stages or groups.
Their confession of two deaths and two lives continues that contrary final speech.
The inmates' appeal to Malik and his reply are a later punitive dialogue, again preventing an absolute reading of 77:35.
Close friends do not ask about one another, supporting the collapse of normal reciprocal support in the final crisis.
The absence of vain speech or falsehood in the rewarded setting provides a measured contrast to judgmental speech restrictions.
Every soul knows what it has brought, expressing the completed self-disclosure that makes denial untenable.
The recipient of the adverse record calls for destruction, a contrary utterance after record disclosure.
